issues.legal_issue: A revenue sale of property in a court-appointed receiver’s custody is illegal when it proceeds without the appointing court’s leave and without notice to the receiver.
material_facts: A receiver appointed by a court had effective control and management of the property when revenue authorities attached and sold it to recover arrears.
The revenue authorities knew that the receiver was in charge of the property, but neither obtained leave from the appointing court nor gave notice to the receiver.
The receiver later sued for a declaration and consequential relief concerning the sale.
issues.conclusion: The sale was illegal. The Court did not decide whether it was void ab initio and proceeded on the assumption that it was voidable.
issues.legal_principle: Property held in custodia legis by a court-appointed receiver is generally protected from proceedings by other authorities unless the appointing court gives leave; this rule prevents conflicts of jurisdiction and protects the property for whoever is ultimately found entitled to it. Order 40, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for appointment of a receiver, and Order 21, rule 52 requires attachment of property in a court’s custody by notice to that court or officer. The Court noted that failure to give attachment notice alone does not ordinarily make a sale void, but held that the absence of both leave and the necessary notice made this sale illegal. It also observed that, had leave been obtained or the receiver been served with the demand, the receiver would have been obliged to pay the arrears and the sale would have been subject to the procedures for challenging revenue sales.

rule.if: revenue_sale_proceeding and property_in_receiver_custody and no_appointing_court_leave and receiver_not_notified

predicates.revenue_sale_proceeding: A revenue authority conducted a sale of property to recover public revenue.
predicates.property_in_receiver_custody: A court-appointed receiver had custody and management of the property when the sale proceedings occurred.
predicates.no_appointing_court_leave: The authority proceeded against the property without obtaining leave from the court that appointed the receiver.
predicates.receiver_not_notified: The receiver was not given notice of the relevant demand or sale proceedings.

issues.definition: When a revenue authority sells property held by a court-appointed receiver without the appointing court’s leave and without notifying the receiver, the sale is illegal.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory bar on suits challenging irregularities or mistakes in publishing or conducting a revenue sale does not bar a suit based on other grounds.
material_facts: The receiver challenged a revenue sale of property in the receiver’s custody, relying on the absence of leave from the appointing court and notice to the receiver.
The suit sought a declaration and, after possession had been delivered to the purchaser, consequential relief for recovery of possession.
The suit was not based on fraud or on the assertion that the revenue arrears were not due, and its grounds were not irregularities or mistakes in publishing or conducting the sale.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not barred by section 157 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928.
issues.legal_principle: Section 156 permits an application to set aside a sale for material irregularity or mistake in publishing or conducting it. Section 157(1) bars claims on those grounds if no such application is made within the allowed time; it does not bar claims on other grounds. Section 157(2) expressly saves suits based on fraud or on the ground that the arrears were not due, but does not make the grounds in section 157(1) exhaustive of all possible grounds for suit. The Court recognized that other grounds may fall between the two subsections.

predicates.civil_suit_challenging_revenue_sale: A claimant brought a civil suit challenging a sale conducted by revenue authorities.
predicates.claim_is_outside_sale_publication_or_con: The suit relied on a ground other than irregularity or mistake in publishing or conducting the sale.

issues.definition: A civil suit challenging a revenue sale is not barred on the statutory irregularity-claim ground when it relies on a ground other than irregularity or mistake in publishing or conducting the sale.

issues.legal_issue: The bar on civil suits concerning matters entrusted to revenue authorities does not apply to a suit for declaration and consequential relief on grounds those authorities are not empowered to determine.
material_facts: The receiver’s suit sought a declaration that the sale did not affect the interests held in the receiver’s custody and consequential recovery of possession from the purchaser.
The grounds relied on were not grounds that the revenue authorities were empowered to determine under the procedures for setting aside a sale.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not barred by section 192 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928.
issues.legal_principle: Section 192(1) bars a civil court from entertaining a suit or application seeking a decision on a matter that the Code empowers the Provincial Government or a revenue officer to determine, decide or dispose of. The Code provided revenue authorities with procedures to set aside a sale on specified grounds, including under sections 155 and 156. But the suit at issue was not a suit simpliciter to set aside a sale under those procedures; it sought a declaration and consequential relief on grounds outside the matters entrusted to those authorities.

predicates.civil_suit_concerning_revenue_sale: A claimant brought a civil suit concerning a sale conducted by revenue authorities.
predicates.suit_seeks_declaration_or_consequential_: The suit seeks a declaration concerning the effect of the sale or relief consequential to that declaration.
predicates.grounds_outside_revenue_authority_powers: The grounds for the requested relief are not matters that the revenue authorities are empowered to determine.

issues.definition: A civil suit concerning a revenue sale is not barred when it seeks a declaration or consequential relief on grounds outside the revenue authorities’ powers to determine.
